case_name: Abrar v The State Of Uttar Pradesh
respondent:
The State Of Uttar Pradesh
Supreme Court of India

16 December 2010
Criminal Appeal No. 1668 of 2005
The Judgment was delivered by : H.S. Bedi, J.
1.  At about 9.30 p.m. on the 3rd of April, 1979, Mohd. Ashfaq, a practicing Advocate, residing in Mohalla Kapoorpur of Ghazipur town, was returning home after visiting Suhasini Talkies. As he reached near the house of Saeed Khan, he found the four accused, Mukhtar, Abrar, Mateen and Usman, all armed with country made pistols, standing near the door of the house. Mohd. Ashfaq recognized them in the light of the torch that he was carrying. Apprehending danger, Mohd. Ashfaq ran towards his house which was close by, raising an alarm. The accused chased him shouting at each other that he should be done away with on which Abrar, the appellant herein, fired at him from the rear. The alarm raised by the victim attracted Muzur PW-6, Durga Ram PW-7 and one Bissu to the place of incident and they too saw the shot being fired.

facts: At about 9:30 p.m. on the 3rd of April, 1979, Mohd. Ashfaq, a practicing Advocate, residing in Mohalla Kapoorpur of Ghazipur town, was returning home after visiting Suhasini Talkies.
As he reached near the house of Saeed Khan, he found the four accused, Mukhtar, Abrar, Mateen and Usman, all armed with country made pistols, standing near the door of the house.
Mohd. Ashfaq recognized them in the light of the torch that he was carrying.
Apprehending danger, Mohd. Ashfaq ran towards his house which was close by, raising an alarm.
The accused chased him shouting at each other that he should be done away with on which Abrar, the appellant herein, fired at him from the rear.
issues: Whether the dying declarations of the deceased can be relied upon in the absence of direct and positive role assigned to the accused in the statements?
Whether the discrepancies in the dying declarations are significant enough to discard them?
petitioner_arguments: The two eye witnesses had turned hostile and had not supported the prosecution.
There were several discrepancies inter-se these three statements, they could not be relied upon.

It would not have been possible for the deceased to have recognized the four assailants as there was no evidence to show that he was either carrying a torch or there was any electric light available at the site where he had been shot.
respondent_arguments: The dying declarations were categorical inasmuch that the four accused had been named in each one of them.
There was absolutely no reason to discard the dying declaration recorded by the Tahsildar at 11:50 p.m. after he had taken a certificate from the doctor that the victim's fitness to make a statement.
court_reasoning: The High Court has, by its judgment, which is now impugned before us, reversed that of the trial court holding that the so called discrepancies were insignificant that they could occur in any statement recorded in Court.
The Court also held that if Mukhtar, Mateen and Usman had also been carrying country made pistol, they would in normal circumstances, have used them as well.
The Court observed that there was no bar in relying only on a part of a dying declaration as the only test was the test of reliability.
holding: We are, therefore, of the opinion, that no fault whatsoever could be found in the dying declarations.
It is, accordingly, dismissed. Appeal dismissed.
